extracted.intended_audience: public company registrants (issuers), investors, auditors, and securities counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Official SEC guidance and final-rule text describing what climate-related information registrants must (or need not) disclose, how it should be framed (e.g., time horizons, governance, targets), and legal/procedural protections (e.g., PSLRA safe harbor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of Scope 1 and 2 emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules will require some registrants to disclose their Scope 1 and 2 emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For registrants that already disclose them, the incremental cost will only be the reporting cost (distinct from prior voluntary costs). The rules enable registrants to continue to use the operational and organizational boundaries they already use to track emissions. The staff notes, however, that many registrants do not fully measure Scope 1 emissions and that existing emissions data quality can be an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope 3 emissions not required
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules will not require disclosure of Scope 3 emissions information, including in the context of a registrant's targets or goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reiterates that Scope 3 is excluded from required disclosures under the final rules (see section II.H.2 references). Comment letters and stakeholders on both sides are noted, but the rule does not mandate Scope 3 reporting here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition plan disclosure (if adopted)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant must disclose, if it has adopted a transition plan (i.e., a strategy and implementation plan to reduce climate-related risks) as part of its climate-related risk management strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to facilitate investor understanding of whether a company has a plan and whether it may be effective in the short, medium, and long term. Commenters (e.g., CFA Institute) support disclosure of transition plans because it helps evaluate actions and potential effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario analysis disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of scenario analysis to describe the resilience of a company's strategy and implications for enterprise value and value chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites external guidance (e.g., C2ES Using Scenarios; FRB Climate Stress Testing) and investor letters saying scenario analysis is a useful tool. The rule treats scenario analysis disclosures as informative for investors assessing resilience under different climate scenarios; forward-looking scenario analysis may be eligible for PSLRA safe harbor protections (see safe_harbor criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: PSLRA safe harbor for forward-looking climate statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward-looking statements related to transition plans, scenario analysis, internal carbon pricing, and climate-related targets and goals will have the benefit of PSLRA safe harbor protections if the safe harbor requirements are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The safe harbor may reduce litigation risk and related costs (and potentially insurance costs). The Commission notes this coverage applies to registration statements in IPOs as well, lowering litigation exposure for forward-looking disclosures described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance disclosure: board oversight and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhancements to disclosure on governance to help investors assess whether the issuer is appropriately considering climate-related risks, including board accountability and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule emphasizes that boards should be able to articulate how material climate-related risks are identified and integrated into governance philosophy; inability to do so is a 'significant red flag' for investors. The board's accountability and the need for independent assurance are noted as important governance elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: MD&A timeframes for climate-related matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate-related matters should be addressed within the same short- and long-term time frames used in MD&A (short-term = next 12 months; long-term = beyond next 12 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 17 CFR 229.303(b)(1) and investor/commenter support (e.g., ABA). The guidance instructs registrants to analyze ability to generate/obtain cash in both the short- and long-term in the context of climate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting costs: definition and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting costs refer to the costs of preparing information to be presented in Commission filings, separate from any prior costs or resources expended in obtaining or developing such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For registrants that already disclose certain climate information (e.g., Scope 1 and 2), only the incremental cost of including that information in Commission filings is considered a reporting cost and is distinct from prior voluntary costs of developing measurement/estimation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary costs consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietary costs are generally relevant for reporting that involves information about a company's business operations or production processes and disclosures that are specific, detailed and process-oriented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission acknowledges proprietary cost concerns particularly where disclosures could reveal competitively sensitive operational details; commenters raised these concerns in relation to certain granular reporting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline selection and 'cherry-picking' of baseline years
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuers tend to 'cherry-pick' the baseline year (i.e., pick the year with highest emissions within the past few years) when forming an emissions target so that any progress appears in the most favorable light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rules will help investors identify when such cherry-picking occurs so they can more accurately assess progress toward targets or goals. The Commission cites research (e.g., NBER Working Paper) documenting this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of operational and organizational boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules enable registrants to continue to use the operational and organizational boundaries they already use to track emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design choice aims to limit costs for registrants that already track and disclose emissions, by allowing continuity in measurement and reporting systems rather than forcing new boundary definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of management's plans and progress on targets/goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants should disclose management's plans to address climate risks, including how management is meeting or not meeting the targets or goals in those plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters emphasized these disclosures as essential for investors and market participants to evaluate the effectiveness of management actions and to understand progress toward stated targets or goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-useful disclosure: complete, reliable, and consistent information
rubrics_metrics.description: Investors need disclosure of climate risks that is complete, reliable, and consistent in order to analyze how climate-related risks may affect a company's business or overall financial performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investor letters (e.g., PIMCO, Wellington, AllianceBernstein) stress that standardized, comparable disclosures improve investors' ability to price risks and make capital allocation decisions; lack of comparability and verification in voluntary regimes is cited as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPO and business-combination-specific treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain provisions reduce costs for conducting an IPO (e.g., registrants will only have to provide Article 14 disclosure for historical fiscal years on a prospective basis), and the PSLRA safe harbor for forward-looking statements will apply to registration statements in IPOs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission also notes that investors will not have the benefit of the final rules' disclosures with respect to private companies in business combination transactions where the private company information is not required, which is a tradeoff acknowledged in the rule.
